args.text: ### Project Directory Setup Strewth, where do I start? With a directory, that's where: somewhere to keep yer Rust code. Now, Rust itself doesn't give a toss where yer code lives, it's not fussy, but for the exercises and projects in this book we reckon ya make a _projects_ directory in yer home directory and keep the whole lot in there, nice and tidy. So fire up a terminal and punch in these commands. They'll make ya a _projects_ directory, and a directory for the “Hello, world!” project sittin' inside the _projects_ directory. Linux, macOS, and PowerShell on Windows mob, this one's yours: ```console $ mkdir ~/projects $ cd ~/projects $ mkdir hello_world $ cd hello_world ``` And for the Windows CMD crowd, it's this lot: ```cmd > mkdir "%USERPROFILE%\projects" > cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\projects" > mkdir hello_world > cd hello_world ``` ### Rust Program Basics Righto, next ya make a new source file and call it _main.rs_. Rust files always end in the _.rs_ extension, no exceptions. And if yer filename's got more than one word in it, the convention is an underscore between 'em, so it's _hello_world.rs_, not _helloworld.rs_, which just looks like someone sat on the keyboard. Now crack open that _main.rs_ file ya just made and type in the code in Listing 1-1. Three lines. That's the lot. ```rust fn main() { println!("Hello, world!"); } ``` Save the file and duck back to yer terminal window in the _~/projects/hello_world_ directory. On Linux or macOS, punch in these commands to compile and run the file: ```console $ rustc main.rs $ ./main Hello, world! ``` On Windows, mind, it's the command `.\main` instead of `./main`, cos Windows always has to be different: ```powershell > rustc main.rs > .\main Hello, world! ``` Whatever operatin' system yer on, the string `Hello, world!` oughta pop up in the terminal. If ya don't see that output, don't spit the dummy: have a squiz back at the [“Troubleshooting”][troubleshooting] part of the Installation section for ways to get some help. And if `Hello, world!` did print? Good on ya, ya legend! Ya've officially written a Rust program. That makes ya a Rust programmer. Welcome to the club, mate, first round's on you.
